entry.evidence: Here and in general, the chemistry of the water is scarcely present in studies of the earthquake preparation process.

steps.action: Summarises published laboratory work on microcrack development, dilatancy and permeability increase as the initial stage of earthquake preparation.
steps.quote: the opening of micro fractures represents the initial stage of the earthquake preparation process

steps.action: Poses the gap that water chemistry is largely absent from earthquake-preparation models, which treat water as a physical agent, and sets the aim of integrating water chemistry with physical models.
steps.quote: the chemistry of the water is scarcely present in studies of the earthquake preparation process

steps.action: Takes from fault-valving simulations and earlier work the expectation of a pore-pressure cycle (drop at microcrack opening, rise during nucleation).
steps.quote: during inter-seismic periods a complete cycle with a pressure decrease and an increase may occur

steps.action: States the working hypothesis that microcrack-induced depressurisation perturbs the water-rock chemical equilibrium and exposes fresh rock surfaces to the destabilised water.
steps.quote: a consequence never taken into consideration is that the opening of microcracks creates perturbations in the water–rock equilibrium

steps.action: Compiles published data on water hydrogen bonding, density and compressibility from standard to supercritical conditions (Figs. 1-2), choosing density as the macroscale descriptor.
steps.quote: small isothermal variations of pressure yield substantial changes in density

steps.action: Uses Yoshii et al.'s molecular dynamics results (Table 1) showing the dielectric constant of supercritical water falling with density along the 427 °C isotherm.
steps.quote: In a simulation the same authors observed the behaviour of water

steps.action: Compiles density-solubility relations for quartz, NaCl and calcite in supercritical water, refitting or recomputing curves (Fig. 3, calcite from Eq. 3), and assumes mineral solubility stands for rock solubility.
steps.quote: highlighting the density-solubility correlation experimentally found and/or calculated with SCW

steps.action: Adopts the stress-corrosion and silanol-formation models (Anderson and Grew; Michalske and Freiman; Parks) for water-assisted subcritical crack growth in quartz.
steps.quote: explain the slow crack propagation with the mechanism of the stress corrosion

steps.action: Uses Rimsza et al.'s molecular dynamics result that water lowers silica fracture toughness by about 25%.
steps.quote: The role of the water in this process lowers the fracture toughness by about 25% in the entire fracture process

steps.action: Merges the water state diagram with a hydrostatic crustal profile for 25 and 40 °C/km gradients, defining the critical depth and the supercritical-water zone bounded by the brittle-ductile transition (Fig. 6).
steps.quote: It starts from a static situation by merging a generic earth crust profile with the water state diagram.

steps.action: Proposes the liquid-phase branch: weak pressure dependence of solubility unless vaporisation occurs, with separation of CO2, H2 and CH4 into a multiphase system.
steps.quote: if there is no liquid/vapour phase transition, pressures correlate weakly with ion solubility

steps.action: Reports a PHREEQC simulation of hot pressurised low-ionic-strength water with granite showing low pressure dependence and secondary clay and OH-bearing mineral formation.

Proposes the three-stage supercritical pressure cycle (equilibrium; depressurisation with loss of polar properties and precipitation; repressurisation with aggressive dissolution and enhanced crack growth) leading to rock weakening and an earlier main shock.
steps.quote: as the fluid pressure increases, minerals solubilities rise, in some cases exponentially, with increasing density

steps.action: Sets the liquid versus supercritical weakening contrast against Takahashi and Hashida's triaxial granite tests, which showed strength loss at or above the critical temperature.
steps.quote: The results show a net and rapid strength decrease as the water temperature is equal or above critical value.

steps.action: Summarises published traces of the 2009 L'Aquila preparation phase: Vp/Vs variations, dilatancy and fluid diffusion, deep CO2 discharge, and pressurised fluids before the mainshock.
steps.quote: Di Luccio et al. (15) explain the observed Vp/Vs variations with the action of moving deep fluids

steps.action: Applies the model qualitatively to L'Aquila, assuming liquid water in a CO2-saturated carbonate system: CO2 separation and calcite precipitation at dilatancy, then acid dissolution at repressurisation.
steps.quote: The complex sequence of dilatancy and fluid diffusion offers instead a basis that may explain the mentioned cracking

steps.action: Offers an alternative to Chiodini et al.'s thermal mechanism for the surface CO2 discharge: release of supercritical CO2 by depressurisation during dilatancy.
steps.quote: The present model also provides a different explanation on CO2 discharge at surface.

steps.action: Computes from published CO2 solubility models the scCO2 released by a 10 MPa depressurisation from 150 °C and 60 MPa.
steps.quote: a depressurisation of 10 MPa produces the release of about 20 g of scCO2 per 1000 g of H2O

steps.action: Retains the chemical weakening model as a working hypothesis integrating physical models, while noting that further investigation is needed for L'Aquila.
steps.quote: the chemical action of water could become of primary importance in causing further weakening of the rocks

No; water chemistry at depth is not observed, only inferred from lab and simulation data
Explain the chemical role of liquid and supercritical water in rock weakening
Purely physical (effective-pressure) water models; Chiodini's thermal CO2 mechanism
Found, not set: the past L'Aquila 2009 event, known from published traces

tree.answer: No; a single event is used
Not tested; no variation or replication
Four anonymous reviewers acknowledged; no review file supplied

end.claim: Once microfracturing begins, the pressure cycle on pore water, especially supercritical water, chemically weakens rock through density-tuned solubility changes and water-assisted subcritical crack growth, possibly favouring the main shock.

decisive_move.sentence: The three-stage supercritical-water pressure-cycle mechanism, built on the compiled density-solubility relations and the Fig. 6 state diagram, is what constitutes the claim.

gates.evidence: No new data were acquired; all evidence is compiled from published lab, simulation and field studies (Data availability: data from published papers and NIST, p. 1218). The model is not tested against an outcome that could falsify it; the L'Aquila application is qualitative and 'preliminary' (§5 ¶1, §5 ¶5). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Molecular dynamics simulations of water hydrogen bonding and dielectric constant (Kalinichev and Bass; Yoshii et al.)
Decomposition of the dielectric constant into dipole moment and orientational correlation G_K
Ion-pairing models (contact ion pair, solvent-separated ion pair) for NaCl in supercritical water
Michalske and Freiman molecular model of stress corrosion in silica (silanol formation)
Polar properties of high-density supercritical water from corrosion studies (Kritzer)
National Institute of Standards and Technology water property data

novelty_claims.quote: This work defines for the first time the chemical mechanisms that take place in the hypocentral zone during the earthquake preparation process
a consequence never taken into consideration is that the opening of microcracks creates perturbations in the water–rock equilibrium

limits: The paper is a conceptual synthesis: every quantitative input is taken from published experiments or simulations, and the model yields no prediction tested against data; hence no V steps and an empty v_checks list (V = none). The outcome is coded kept/best_explanation for lack of a closer status: the claim is a working hypothesis ('it is likely'; 'working hypothesis', §6 ¶2), not singled out against rivals by a test. Composition none_fits because there is no crucial test, no repeated traces, no new capability and no exploration. Only one stated rival is engaged directly (Chiodini et al.'s CO2 mechanism); physical-only models are integrated rather than excluded. Sub-claims: the critical-depth/BDT zone of supercritical water (Fig. 6) is a derived expectation from known phase relations; the L'Aquila account is a qualitative reconstruction that assumes liquid water, so the supercritical branch is not applied to the example. The author assumes mineral solubility stands for rock solubility (§3 ¶2), neglects ionic content, assumes hydrostatic pressure and assumes free water at depth. Inference: it is unclear whether the PHREEQC simulation (§4.1 ¶3) was run by the author, since no results source is cited; it is coded as performed here. The calcite curve in Fig. 3C is computed by the author from Eq. 3; the printed equation contains an apparent typographical oddity '(32.8 − 0.028)' (inference: probably a missing T term). Four anonymous reviewers are acknowledged, but no review file is supplied, so revisions from review cannot be coded.

disagreements.target: Yamashita and Tsutsumi (2018): presence of water at depth is ubiquitous
disagreements.support: Notes that free water at depth is documented only at specific sites (Kola, KTB boreholes), so its presence everywhere cannot be assumed.
disagreements.quote: Actually, there is no assurance that water at depth is present everywhere

disagreements.target: Models treating water only as a physical agent (e.g. Miller 2013; Yoshida and Hasegawa 2018)
disagreements.support: Argues from compiled solubility and crack-growth literature that water also acts chemically, and claims to integrate rather than replace physical models.
disagreements.quote: [...] the general conception of other models based on the notion that water is only a physical agent

disagreements.target: Chiodini et al. (2020): thermal mechanism of deep CO2 release and discharge at L'Aquila
disagreements.support: A back-of-envelope scCO2 solubility calculation shows that depressurisation during dilatancy would release scCO2, offered as an alternative explanation; no test between the two is made.
disagreements.quote: The present model also provides a different explanation on CO2 discharge at surface.
